title: Ribollita
subtitle: Tuscan bread and bean soup
excerpt: Ribollita means 'reboiled' in Italian -- it was made to use up leftover minestrone the next day, thickened with stale bread. This version is made from scratch but follows the same principle: a hearty bean and cavolo nero soup finished with torn bread until it thickens. It improves overnight.
sourceNotes: A peasant soup from Tuscany, Italy. The name means 'reboiled.' It was traditionally made on Friday from leftover Thursday minestrone, thickened with stale bread and reheated.

recipe.batchNotes: Makes excellent leftovers. The soup thickens further overnight and is even better reheated.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead for best flavour. Reheat gently with a splash of water.

content.text: Use the darkest, most robust leaves of cavolo nero you can find. Strip the leaves from the tough central stalks before using. Stale bread works best -- fresh bread turns gluey.

items.prepNote: use stale ciabatta or sourdough, torn into chunks

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 10 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic and rosemary. Cook for 2 minutes.
Add the tinned tomatoes and stock. Bring to a simmer.
Add the cavolo nero. Cook for 15 minutes.
Mash about a third of the beans with a fork. Add all the beans to the pot.
Stir in the torn bread. Cook for 10 more minutes, stirring often, until the soup thickens.
Remove the rosemary stalks. Season well and serve with a generous drizzle of olive oil.

items.cause: Bread absorbed more liquid than expected
items.fix: Add hot stock or water and stir. Ribollita should be very thick, almost like a stew.
Add more salt and a good drizzle of olive oil. Olive oil carries a lot of flavour here.

content.text: Ribollita is from Tuscany, where it has been made for centuries as a way to use leftover bean soup and stale bread. The name refers to the tradition of reboiling yesterday's soup with fresh bread to create something even heartier. It is now served in restaurants across Italy as a winter speciality. A drizzle of good olive oil on top is not optional.
